topic: Myth-bust: Jev's 312-to-1 speedup comes from parallel constrained decoding, reproducible on a stock Qwen-2.5-1.5B checkpoint on one MacBook, with zero new training.
title: Jev Speed Myth: Stock Qwen Already Has the Trick
description:
Everyone assumes Jev's speed comes from exotic new weights. An open replication (harshatheg/Qwen-2.5-1B-RLCD, Apache 2.0) reproduces the launch numbers with the stock mlx-community Qwen2.5-1.5B checkpoint running through MLX on one M4 Max MacBook, using parallel constrained decoding instead of new training. All measurements are the replication author's published runs. Full episode: https://youtube.com/@BuildLocalAI
(Narration is AI-generated.)
hook_candidates: Jev's speed isn't in the weights. Your Qwen already has it.
Three moves and the Jev trick runs on your Mac tonight.
One pass instead of three hundred twelve. Stock Qwen weights.
You watched it type JSON one word at a time. Stop asking it to write.
A 28-field form went from 1,900 ms to 270 ms on a MacBook.
TypeSafe's Jev, rebuilt with the Qwen you already downloaded.
Your chat model can't write. That's the feature.
The menu trick that made a small model fast.
Qwen-2.5 plus one decoding trick equals Jev's numbers.
narration_full: Jev's speed isn't in the weights. Your Qwen already has it. Three hundred twelve forward passes become one. You run a small open model like Qwen two point five in Ollama or LM Studio. You've watched it type JSON one word at a time. The myth says that speed lives in exotic weights no home machine could serve. Yesterday TypeSafe released Jev, the first System One Model. It gives up writing text and returns structured values with calibrated probabilities, honest scores of how sure it is. Yet an open replication on Hugging Face hits those numbers. It's free under the Apache license, and it runs the stock Qwen checkpoint you can already download. No new training. One MacBook. The win is in how you decode, not what you train. You write a schema beforehand: the list of fields and their allowed answers. The test form has twenty-eight fields. Each is a boolean, a yes or no, or an enum, a fixed menu of choices. The old way writes an essay, one token, a chunk of a word, at a time. The new way is a scantron sheet. Every bubble at the same instant. The limit: a scantron chooses with no doubt, the engine returns a probability for every option. It's called parallel constrained decoding, every field answered in one pass. The prompt is prefilled once into a KV cache, the model's short-term memory, and shared across all fields. Each field scores only its own candidate tokens. The rest of the vocabulary is masked off. On the replication author's M four Max MacBook, this form took nineteen hundred milliseconds the old way. The new decoding took two hundred seventy milliseconds. Sequential forward passes, full trips through the model, fell from three hundred twelve to one. Another belief to drop: structured output isn't asking the model to please answer in JSON. The model never writes the JSON. Code assembles it. So the shape is valid every single time, by construction. But guaranteed shape is not guaranteed truth. A valid answer can still be a wrong answer. A one point five billion parameter model can flip a boolean between runs. Route low-confidence fields to a human or a bigger model. The myth survives in one place: weights decide what a model knows, so judgment needs a stronger model. For typed answers, the speed was never in the weights. It was in refusing to let the model write.

analogy.mapping: autoregressive decoding is writing an essay one word at a time; parallel constrained decoding is bubbling one option per question with every bubble filled at the same instant; vocabulary masking makes a stray mark outside the bubbles impossible
analogy.limit: a scantron picks one bubble with no doubt, while the engine returns a full probability for every option

notes_for_review:
1) Constraint conflict: the verbatim two-sentence hook pushes the spoken measurement to about 4.2 s; "312 → 1" is on screen from about 1.5 s so the measurement lands visually before second 4. The viewer situation lands in sentences four to five for the same reason.
2) Only the three cleared measured numbers are spoken (312-to-1 passes, nineteen hundred milliseconds, two hundred seventy milliseconds), attributed to the replication author's M four Max run; "twenty-eight fields", "one point five billion", "M four Max", and "Qwen two point five" are referents or product names.
3) Verify narration_full matches the scene narrations exactly, and that every on-screen digit has a spoken counterpart in its scene (repo id and license version were deliberately kept off screen).
